one_liner: C11 bulk random-variate library (xoshiro/PCG/Philox/ChaCha, 20+ distributions); ~10-15x faster than C++ <random> for U(0,1)/N(0,1) fills.
what_it_does: A C library that fills caller arrays with variates: raw bits, bounded integers, permutations, sampling without replacement, uniform, normal, gamma, beta, t, F, Weibull and more, plus multivariate normal. The API is array-oriented (randompack_norm(x, n, rng)) with an opaque randompack_rng handle created by engine name, NumPy-style seed_seq_fe128 seeding with spawn keys, jumps, and state serialization. It is not a drop-in for std::uniform_random_bit_generator; C++ uses it through an extern "C" header. Output streams are bit-identical across platforms for U(0,1), N(0,1), Exp(1) and integers.
how_it_is_fast: Bulk generation through an internal 144-word (1152-byte) buffer and tight inlined loops instead of one virtual-ish call per sample. The default engine x256++simd runs eight xoshiro256++ streams in parallel on AVX2, AVX-512 or NEON (unrolled scalar fallback elsewhere). Normals use a 256-strip ziggurat (Marsaglia-Tsang with McFarland's 2016 refinements), uniforms use a 52-bit mantissa bit trick, and vectorized log/exp come from Sleef.
when_to_use: Filling large arrays (thousands+) of U(0,1), normal, exponential or gamma variates in Monte Carlo or simulation code where std::mt19937_64 + <random> distributions dominate the profile.

Projects that need the same stream across C, C++, Fortran, Python, R and Julia, or across x86-64, ARM and Windows/macOS/Linux (bit-identical for the core distributions, optional bitexact mode for the rest).
Parallel simulations needing reproducible independent substreams (spawn keys, jumps, Philox/squares keys) and checkpoint/restart via state serialization.
Code that wants a choice of engines behind one API, including ChaCha20 when a cryptographically secure generator is required.
when_not_to_use: One-at-a-time draws inside a hot loop: the speed comes from bulk fills, and per-call use (n=1) does not get the buffered/SIMD benefit (only bulk timings are published).
If you already have oneMKL: the paper reports MKL faster for U(0,1) (about 1.3x) and for some distributions such as beta and gamma; Julia is on par for normals and faster for permutations/sampling.
If you need a header-only or std::-compatible URBG to plug into existing <random> code or templates.
If you need a mature, widely used dependency: young project (0.1.x, first release 2026), 3 stars, single author, paper submitted to ACM TOMS but not yet peer reviewed.
Non-bitexact mode gives tolerance (about 2 ulp) rather than bit reproducibility for secondary distributions; bitexact mode costs 2-4x on some distributions.

integration.form: shared lib (Meson/Ninja build, default_library=shared; also conda-forge librandompack)
integration.dependencies: Meson >= 1.3, Ninja, pkg-config; BLAS/LAPACK for multivariate normal (Accelerate/OpenBLAS/MKL auto-detected, bundled reference fallback); README says a Fortran compiler is required for the source build; uses OpenLibm-derived transcendental code and Sleef vector math per the paper
integration.min_toolchain: C11 compiler (clang, gcc, icx, MSVC, nvc tested); C++17 for the C++ benchmark
integration.platforms: x86-64 (AVX2/AVX-512 paths), aarch64/NEON (Apple M, Linux ARM), Windows; scalar fallback without SIMD or 128-bit multiply; requires 32-bit int and 64-bit long long
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe if each thread uses its own rng object; no global state

gotchas: meson.build defaults to buildtype=debug; pass --buildtype=release (as the README and scripts/meson-setup.sh do) or the benchmarked speed will not appear.
The default engine is x256++simd (eight interleaved xoshiro256++ streams), so its output is not the same sequence as a scalar xoshiro256++ with the same seed.
For Philox and squares, do not change the counter via randompack_set_state while in use; the library advances counters internally as it fills buffers.
Multivariate normal is double precision only and pulls in BLAS/LAPACK.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Randompack when you need full distributions (normal, gamma, beta, etc.) in bulk with cross-language reproducibility; SIMDxorshift and Randen only give raw bits, and cxx-ziggurat covers only the normal distribution as a header-only C++ piece. Use Randen when you need backtracking-resistant output with an std-compatible C++ engine.
verified_claims_summary: On an Intel Core i5-1335U with clang, the author's paper (Table 8) reports bulk U(0,1) at 0.42 ns/value vs 6.3 for C++ std::mt19937_64 + uniform_real_distribution (~15x) and N(0,1) at 1.4 vs 14.3 ns/value for std::normal_distribution (~10x); NumPy, Julia and MKL are also listed, with Julia and MKL close. The C++ comparison code (benchmark/TimeDistCpp.cpp) is public; the C++ standard library and clang version are not stated.
status_note: Actively maintained (0.1.11 on 2026-08-27, frequent releases with PyPI, CRAN, Julia and conda-forge packaging); MIT-licensed and copyable, but young and single-author.
